title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
authors: Mahish K. Guru, Mayank Nagar, Ayush vyas, Jan Bohlen, Roland Aydin, Noomane Ben Khalifa
abstract: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

infographic.key_insight: Co-PiLOT solves inverse design by searching in a learned latent space, where a decoder acts as a validity prior and physics-informed optimization guides candidates toward the target microstructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For magnesium alloy microstructure/texture design, this provides a practical way to reduce expensive crystal plasticity simulations while still enforcing feasibility and target-driven performance.
method: ViT-based encoder compresses EBSD microstructures into a low-dimensional latent code.
Generative decoders (latent diffusion, DiT, rectified-flow) reconstruct high-fidelity candidate microstructures.
MERIDIAN performs active latent optimization with deep-kernel GP uncertainty, feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an ~80,000-image EBSD dataset, ViT-FMDiT achieved the strongest reconstruction quality reported (FID 27.86) and, with MERIDIAN, achieved the best target-driven objective under a budget of 160 simulations, reducing relative target error by 3–22% versus seven baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on decoder fidelity and solver-in-the-loop simulation budget, so performance may degrade if the learned latent manifold does not faithfully cover rare but important feasible microstructures.
infographic.paper_title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design

title: Fracture of Lattice Materials from Low to High Relative Density
authors: Adam P. Taylor, Sage Fulco, Kevin T. Turner
abstract: Lattice materials have highly tunable mechanical properties that are controlled by their internal geometry and base material behavior. While fracture models for low-density lattices are well-established, the fracture of lattices at relative densities above 30% remains largely unexplored. Here, we present an analytical model that combines homogenization methods and blunt-crack fracture theory to predict the fracture toughness of triangular and hexagonal lattices over a wide range of relative densities. Finite element modeling corroborates the analytical framework and demonstrates a shift in failure mechanisms between low and high relative density regimes. At high relative densities, failure is dominated by nodal stress concentrations, which are strongly influenced by the local crack-tip geometry and the macroscopic crack path. Significant stress redistribution is observed as the relative orientation and lattice fillet radius are varied, resulting in increased fracture toughness relative to baseline geometries. Furthermore, quasi-brittle poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) lattices achieve about a 1.6x enhancement in fracture toughness relative to perfectly brittle lattices as failure is delayed by localized plasticity. Notably, some quasi-brittle lattices are found to exceed the fracture toughness of their base material -- a feature only possible when the cell size is large compared to the base material's plastic radius. Experiments on lattice fracture specimens made from laser-cut PMMA validate the finite element results, but highlight the stochastic nature of failure in brittle lattice materials, especially at higher relative densities.

infographic.key_insight: A unified fracture model shows that lattice materials transition from geometry-controlled low-density fracture to nodal stress-concentration-driven failure at higher relative densities, with crack-tip shape and lattice fillets strongly affecting toughness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designers can use lattice geometry, orientation, and fillet radius to tune fracture toughness across a wide density range, including cases where quasi-brittle lattices can outperform the base material in crack resistance.
method: Homogenization-based analytical model for triangular and hexagonal lattices
Blunt-crack fracture theory extended to higher relative densities
Finite element simulations and laser-cut PMMA experiments for validation
infographic.evidence_signal: The analytical model is corroborated by finite element results and supported by PMMA fracture experiments, which also show roughly 1.6× toughness enhancement in quasi-brittle lattices and a strong dependence of failure on relative density.
infographic.watch_item: Brittle lattice fracture remains stochastic, so high-density predictions may be sensitive to local crack-path details, nodal geometry, and manufacturing variability.
infographic.paper_title: Fracture of Lattice Materials from Low to High Relative Density

title: The Universal Classifier for Graph Learning
authors: Ben Finkelshtein, André Linhares, Petar Veličković, Bryan Perozzi, Mikhail Galkin
abstract: While foundation models have revolutionized natural language processing and computer vision by leveraging universal vocabularies, Graph Machine Learning (GML) remains fractured due to the absence of a unified feature and structural representation across diverse domains. Existing works claiming to be Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) are typically restricted to node-level predictions or require fixed feature dimensions, failing to provide a truly task-agnostic backbone for the full spectrum of graph learning applications. In this paper, we introduce the Universal Classifier (UC), which supports arbitrary feature and class cardinalities, unifying node-, edge-, and graph-level objectives under a single similarity-based classification objective. The UC reformulates all node-, edge-, and graph-level prediction tasks as maximizing similarity in the latent space: by lifting heterogeneous features and labels into 3D latent tensors, the model learns transferable features independent of specific input schemas. This architecture allows a single pre-trained model to generalize to node classification, node regression, and link prediction across unseen graphs with varying feature semantics. Experiments show strong zero-shot transfer performance across node-, link-, and graph-level tasks.

infographic.key_insight: The Universal Classifier unifies node-, edge-, and graph-level learning into one similarity-based framework that can handle arbitrary feature and class sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could simplify graph-based modeling pipelines in engineering by enabling a single pretrained model to transfer across different graph tasks and data schemas.
method: Lifts heterogeneous features and labels into 3D latent tensors
Uses a shared similarity maximization objective for node, edge, and graph prediction
Supports node classification, node regression, and link prediction on unseen graphs
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong zero-shot transfer performance across node-, link-, and graph-level tasks in experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the latent tensor representation and similarity objective scale to very large or highly irregular graphs with changing label semantics.
infographic.paper_title: The Universal Classifier for Graph Learning

title: PoliVEM: a Python-driven virtual element framework for computational solid mechanics
authors: Paulo Akira F. Enabe, Rodrigo Provasi
abstract: This work presents PoliVEM, a software framework for the Virtual Element Method (VEM) in computational solid and structural mechanics. A C++17 computational core and a Python interface place one-dimensional beams, two- and three-dimensional elasticity, axisymmetric elasticity, transient diffusion, and finite-strain hyperelasticity in a common implementation. The framework stores vertex, edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom in one hierarchy, constructs the energy, strain, and $L^2$ projections from common polynomial data, and retains the consistency--stabilization split at the element level. The core separates the mesh, material, element, assembler, and solver responsibilities and combines them by composition. A new formulation supplies its projection, discrete form, and stabilization while reusing the mesh representation, degree-of-freedom numbering, boundary-condition treatment, sparse assembly, algebraic solvers, and Python binding pattern. The numerical infrastructure includes polygonal and polyhedral mesh input, higher-order entity numbering, cached projection operators, static condensation, coloured sparse assembly, linear solver selection based on the matrix structure, an incremental Newton method with line search and regularization, and explicit and implicit time integration. Three numerical experiments examine the shared implementation through polynomial reproduction, recovery after static condensation, higher-order degree-of-freedom handling, polygonal and polyhedral meshes, patch tests, stiffness spectra, and comparisons with independent finite element calculations. The results verify the common core for the beam and two- and three-dimensional elasticity formulations. They also identify the scaling of high-order polynomial bases on anisotropic cells and the memory required by sparse direct factorizations as the main limitations of the current implementation.

infographic.key_insight: PoliVEM unifies multiple virtual element solid-mechanics formulations in one Python-driven framework by reusing a common C++17 core for meshes, projections, assembly, solvers, and boundary handling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a reusable path to implement and compare beam, elasticity, axisymmetric, diffusion, and hyperelasticity models on polygonal/polyhedral meshes with consistent numerical infrastructure.
method: Shared mesh/DOF hierarchy for vertices, edges, faces, and cells
Common energy, strain, and L2 projections with consistency-stabilization split
Modular composition of mesh, material, element, assembler, and solver components
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments on polynomial reproduction, patch tests, static condensation recovery, higher-order DOF handling, stiffness spectra, and comparisons with independent finite element calculations.
infographic.watch_item: High-order polynomial bases on anisotropic cells and the memory cost of sparse direct factorizations are identified as key implementation limitations.
infographic.paper_title: PoliVEM: a Python-driven virtual element framework for computational solid mechanics

title: Neural topology optimization of ship structures under propulsion machinery vibrations
authors: Shengyu Yan, Muhammad Muztahidul Hakim Zareer, Jasmin Jelovica
abstract: Ship structural vibrations contribute to noise, fatigue, and equipment damage, while dynamic-compliance topology optimization can produce pathological designs near resonance. This study extends neural-reparameterized topology optimization using a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KATO) to forced-vibration design with active input power (AIP) as the objective. Applications include a 100 Hz engine-supporting deck panel and an 18 Hz thruster foundation frame. Helmholtz PDE filtering and Heaviside projection control feature sizes and manufacturing tolerance. Across both deck families, all eight optimized layouts reduce AIP relative to size-optimized references and, after finite-depth extrusion, also achieve lower static compliance. For unrestricted, manufacturing-aware, and stress-aware frame variants, KATO matches GCMMA in AIP within 0.5 dB while yielding 22-36x lower static compliance after matched-volume binary re-analysis. In a near-resonant 300 Hz case, both methods reduce initial AIP by more than 32 dB; KATO maintains a connected design, achieves 59x lower binary static compliance, and reduces maximum AIP over 1-500 Hz by 2.7 dB. KATO runs 6.4-10.4x faster than GCMMA for the implemented stress-aware formulations. The results demonstrate neural AIP-driven topology optimization as an efficient approach for designing connected, feature-size-controlled ship structures with improved forced-vibration performance.

infographic.key_insight: A neural-reparameterized topology optimization method (KATO) can design ship structures that better suppress forced-vibration input power while preserving connectivity and manufacturable feature sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a faster way to optimize ship decks and thruster foundations for lower vibration, noise, fatigue, and equipment damage under realistic propulsion loads.
method: Uses a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KATO) to parameterize topology.
Optimizes active input power (AIP) under forced vibration, with Helmholtz filtering and Heaviside projection for minimum length scale and manufacturability.
Benchmarked against GCMMA on deck panels and thruster foundation frames, including stress-aware and near-resonant cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested ship-structure cases, KATO matched GCMMA in AIP within 0.5 dB, reduced binary static compliance by 22-59x in several comparisons, and ran 6.4-10.4x faster in the implemented stress-aware formulations.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is reported for specific benchmark geometries and formulations, so transferability to other ship structures, load cases, and fabrication constraints still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Neural topology optimization of ship structures under propulsion machinery vibrations

title: Averaging in thermodynamic dislocation theory: general macroscopically uniform stress and strain states
authors: Khanh Chau Le
abstract: The averaging procedure, developed for polycrystalline bars under axially symmetric tension or compression, is extended to arbitrary macroscopically uniform stress and strain states. Starting from the equal probability hypothesis for grain orientations, the mean resolved shear stress and the mean resolved elastic and plastic shear strains are defined as root-mean-square averages over all slip-system orientations. Two exact identities for isotropic orientation averages show that the mean resolved shear stress is proportional to the von Mises equivalent stress, and that the direction of macroscopic plastic flow, obtained from the hypothesis that the plastic slip rate on a system is proportional to the resolved shear stress acting on it, is the stress deviator. The result is an associated $J_2$ flow theory whose hardening law is not fitted but follows from the kinetics of thermally activated dislocation depinning and the evolution equations for the dislocation density and the effective disorder temperature of thermodynamic dislocation theory, written as rates with respect to time so that arbitrary loading paths can be followed. For torsion the theory yields the torque--twist relation of bars and tubes without the classical reductions to a shear stress--strain curve. The parameters for copper are identified jointly from Hopkinson-bar tension, dynamic compression at room and elevated temperatures, and torque--twist records at several twist rates. One set of material parameters, consistent with the earlier compression-only identification, describes tension, compression and torsion from room temperature to $1173$\,K and from $10$ to $2300$\,s$^{-1}$ to $6$\,\% rms over 142 data points; the tension--torsion discrepancy noted by Johnson and Cook is traced to the initial dislocation state of their torsion specimens.

infographic.key_insight: Averaging thermodynamic dislocation theory over grain orientations turns macroscopic plasticity into an associated J2 flow model, with hardening emerging from dislocation kinetics rather than curve fitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a single physics-based constitutive law that can predict tension, compression, and torsion of copper across wide temperatures and strain rates, enabling more reliable solid-mechanics simulations.
method: Assume equal-probability grain orientations and compute root-mean-square averages of resolved shear stress/strain over slip systems.
Use exact isotropic orientation identities to link mean resolved shear stress to von Mises stress and plastic flow direction to the stress deviator.
Write dislocation-density and effective-temperature evolution as time rates so arbitrary loading paths and torsion can be modeled directly.
infographic.evidence_signal: A single parameter set matches 142 data points for copper across tension, compression, and torsion from room temperature to 1173 K and 10 to 2300 s^-1, within about 6% rms.
infographic.watch_item: The predicted torsion response depends on the assumed initial dislocation state, so specimen history and preprocessing must be controlled carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Averaging in thermodynamic dislocation theory: general macroscopically uniform stress and strain states

title: Running error bounds in finite element kernels
authors: Michal Habera, Paul T. Kühner, Matteo Croci, Andreas Zilian
abstract: Rounding errors in finite element computations can lead to a complete loss of accuracy, stalled convergence, and incorrect results. Moreover, the effects of rounding errors accumulated within automatically generated and compiled kernels are difficult to analyze a priori. We present the first software framework for automated rounding error estimation within finite element kernels. The proposed methodology is based on an a posteriori technique called Running Error Analysis (REA), where a forward error estimate is automatically computed concurrently with the value. An open-source implementation is provided for the FEniCS Form Compiler (FFCx), based on a C++ backend for generating type-generic templated kernels over a custom arithmetic type that tracks both the value and its error estimate. We demonstrate REA on two examples. First, we use it to detect catastrophic cancellation in the assembly of a Neo-Hooke hyperelastic model in the small deformation regime. A series expansion circumvents the cancellation problem and the computed error estimates show this. Second, we study the assembly of the Laplace operator on a near-degenerate mesh. We demonstrate that our REA implementation typically incurs only 2-4x performance overhead. Applications of this work include robust reduced-precision computations in embedded systems, numerical debugging of new, possibly ill-conditioned or unstable PDE formulations, and guiding the design of mixed-precision kernels.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces an automated way to estimate floating-point rounding error inside finite element kernels as they run, enabling detection of hidden numerical instability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps engineers build more reliable FEM solvers, especially for ill-conditioned problems, reduced-precision workflows, and debugging compiled kernel code.
method: Wrap kernel arithmetic in a custom type that tracks both value and running forward error.
Integrate Running Error Analysis (REA) into the FEniCS Form Compiler (FFCx) via a C++ backend.
Compute error estimates concurrently with kernel values during assembly.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports two demonstrations—catastrophic cancellation in Neo-Hooke assembly and a near-degenerate Laplace mesh case—and states the implementation typically adds only 2-4x runtime overhead.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds nontrivial runtime overhead and depends on compiler/backend integration, so deployment cost and kernel compatibility need care.
infographic.paper_title: Running error bounds in finite element kernels

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Multilayer Planar Winding Inductance Estimation
authors: Spyros Rigas, Theofilos Papadopoulos, Georgios Alexandridis, Antonios Antonopoulos
abstract: Rapid and accurate self-inductance estimation for multilayer rectangle-shaped planar windings is essential for modern high-frequency power converters, yet traditional workflows rely on complex mathematical equations, rigid monomial formulas or unexplainable black-box machine learning (ML) models that degrade severely outside their training domain. This paper introduces an explainable ML framework unifying post-hoc feature attribution (SHAP and permutation importance) with Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-guided symbolic regression via the SR-KAN framework to discover closed-form analytical equations without prior structural assumptions. Evaluated on a new open-source dataset of over 10,000 Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations across seven out-of-distribution (OOD) classes, standard tree-based ensembles exhibit severe extrapolation errors (> 36%), whereas the unconstrained SR-KAN expression achieves a robust OOD relative error of 8.22%. Experimental verification across 55 physical printed circuit board prototypes (up to 8 layers, with inductances from 4.11 μH to 559.27 μH) confirms that the KAN-discovered expression translates effectively to real-world hardware, predicting inductance with a mean absolute relative error of 6.26%. To support reproducible research, the complete FEA simulation dataset and prototype measurements are released open-source.

infographic.key_insight: An explainable ML pipeline can learn a closed-form inductance equation that generalizes far better than conventional black-box models for multilayer planar windings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more reliable inductance estimation for high-frequency power converter design, reducing dependence on expensive FEM sweeps and rigid empirical formulas.
method: Post-hoc explainability with SHAP and permutation importance to rank influential winding features.
SR-KAN symbolic regression to discover an analytical expression without assuming a predefined formula form.
Validation on both large OOD FEM cases and physical PCB prototypes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study used over 10,000 FEA simulations across seven OOD classes and 55 PCB prototypes, with SR-KAN reaching 8.22% OOD relative error and 6.26% mean absolute relative error on hardware.
infographic.watch_item: The discovered formula is data-driven and should still be checked carefully when moving to winding geometries or materials beyond the reported dataset.
infographic.paper_title: Explainable Machine Learning for Multilayer Planar Winding Inductance Estimation

title: FracGen: Learning How Objects Stretch and Tear with Physics-Informed Video Generation
authors: Trong-Tung Nguyen, Jiahan Zhang, Anand Bhattad
abstract: We introduce FracGen, a fracture-aware video generation model that produces plausible, controllable fracture dynamics from a single image of an intact object, conditioned on physics signals. To train FracGen, we build FracSim, a fracture-aware simulation framework that augments material point method (MPM) simulation with a continuum damage model, producing paired fracture videos and dense, pixel-aligned physical fields at no additional cost beyond standard rendering. FracGen leverages these maps in two ways: it is trained to jointly predict them alongside RGB video, encouraging the model to capture physical state rather than surface appearance; and it is supervised with physics-informed losses that encourage consistency among the predicted maps. As a result, FracGen captures distinct material-specific fracture behavior without expensive test-time simulation or per-scene tuning, while offering fine-grained control over where an object tears, how fast the crack propagates, and how much deformation precedes failure. We further introduce a benchmark for evaluating the physical plausibility of generated fracture video, and show through extensive experiments that FracGen outperforms existing video generation baselines in both physical and visual fidelity. Results are best viewed in our project website: https://fracgen.github.io/.

infographic.key_insight: FracGen learns physically plausible fracture video generation from a single intact image by conditioning on dense physics signals so it can predict how objects deform, crack, and tear.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers controllable, material-aware fracture prediction that could support faster virtual testing, design exploration, and damage visualization without expensive per-scene simulation.
method: Builds FracSim, a simulation pipeline that combines MPM with a continuum damage model to generate paired fracture videos and dense physical fields.
Trains FracGen to jointly predict RGB video and physical maps, forcing the model to represent underlying mechanics rather than only appearance.
Uses physics-informed losses to keep predicted fracture fields mutually consistent and controllable during generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a new benchmark for physical plausibility and states that experiments show FracGen outperforms prior video generation baselines in both physical and visual fidelity.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on high-quality simulated fracture-field supervision, so real-world transfer and robustness to unseen materials or loading conditions may still be challenging.
infographic.paper_title: FracGen: Learning How Objects Stretch and Tear with Physics-Informed Video Generation

title: Behavioral Convergence Without Representational Convergence: Persistent Training-History Dependence in Neural Networks
authors: Ertuğrul Mutlu
abstract: Neural networks trained toward the same final objective can reach similar predictive performance while retaining internal representations shaped by earlier training history. We study this effect using controlled sequential-training experiments in which paired convolutional networks start from identical weights, experience reversed task orders, and then receive the same deterministic common-relaxation distribution. Across 20 paired MNIST runs, 16 satisfy a predeclared behavioral-matching criterion, yet their matched representations retain a mean history score of 0.139 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.127-0.153) and approximately 3.1% prediction disagreement. Extending common relaxation to 50,000 optimizer updates does not erase the measured difference: across five paired seeds, the representation-history score remains 0.190 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.161-0.219) at the end of the measured horizon while the mean accuracy gap is only 0.18 percentage points. Fresh linear probes show that, with sufficient labeled data, the two histories retain practically equivalent linearly accessible class information. A same-label rotated-MNIST control reproduces the effect: all five paired seeds reach behavioral matching while retaining a mean representation-history score of 0.162. Finally, a matched-learning-rate ReLU-LeakyReLU control reduces the 50,000-update representation residue by 0.040 on average in all five paired seeds, providing directional evidence that activation-mediated plasticity contributes to the persistence of training-history effects. These results provide protocol-scoped evidence that behavioral convergence need not imply representational convergence and that optimization history can leave measurable internal traces after prolonged common training.

infographic.key_insight: Neural networks can end up behaving similarly on the same final task while still preserving distinct internal representations shaped by their earlier training history.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For constitutive modeling and other predictive systems, matching output accuracy does not guarantee equivalent internal state, so training protocol can leave persistent hidden biases that matter for interpretability and transfer.
method: Paired CNNs start from identical weights but see reversed task orders before a shared deterministic relaxation phase.
Track behavioral matching, prediction disagreement, and a representation-history score across MNIST and rotated-MNIST controls.
Compare against a ReLU-LeakyReLU control and linear-probe access to class information.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 MNIST pairs, 16 met the behavioral-matching criterion, yet matched models still showed a mean history score of 0.139 and about 3.1% prediction disagreement; similar persistence remained after 50,000 updates and in rotated-MNIST controls.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are protocol-scoped, so the persistence of history effects may depend on architecture, activation choice, dataset, and the specific training schedule used.
infographic.paper_title: Behavioral Convergence Without Representational Convergence: Persistent Training-History Dependence in Neural Networks

title: Permeability and microcrack geometry: Dynamic loading induced evolution
authors: Rigoberto Moncada, Efrem Vitali
abstract: We propose a crack-geometry-based model for permeability evolution in rocks under dynamic loading. Accurate representation of permeability is important for fluid extraction and containment in geological formations, but remains challenging because low-porosity brittle rocks are highly sensitive to changes in pore geometry and connectivity, while dynamic permeability measurements are limited. Rock void space is represented as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations. Permeability changes are described through crack microvariables including aperture, length, and crack distance. The model accounts for crack opening and closure, fracture-energy-driven propagation, plastic-strain-driven nucleation, coalescence after full connectivity is reached, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening. The evolving crack network directly modifies connectivity, fluid conductance, and preferential flow paths. The formulation is implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode and evaluated under tension, shear, compression, and symmetric impact loading. Results show a strong relation between permeability and crack length, with crack propagation playing a major role in permeability enhancement. Permeability growth can nevertheless be limited by poor connectivity and crack closure. The model captures changes of several orders of magnitude depending on stress state, strain rate, crack orientation, and connectivity, consistent with observed behavior of brittle rocks under high strain-rate loading.

infographic.key_insight: Permeability in brittle rocks under dynamic loading is governed primarily by how crack geometry evolves—especially crack length, opening, and connectivity—rather than by porosity alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for predicting fluid flow in reservoirs, containment systems, and other geological formations subjected to fast loading or stress changes.
method: Model rock void space as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations.
Update permeability from crack microvariables: aperture, length, and crack spacing/distance.
Include opening/closure, propagation, nucleation, coalescence, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening in the evolution law.
infographic.evidence_signal: Implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode and tested under tension, shear, compression, and symmetric impact, the model reproduced permeability changes spanning several orders of magnitude across stress states and loading rates.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted permeability can be strongly limited by poor crack connectivity or crack closure, so accurate orientation and connectivity inputs are critical for reliable use.
infographic.paper_title: Permeability and microcrack geometry: Dynamic loading induced evolution

title: CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows
authors: Samuel Onimpa Alfred, Abhishek Kumar, Veera Sundararaghavan
abstract: Crystal plasticity (CP) simulations predict the mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals, yet their routine use is hindered by the manual effort of configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experiments. These bottlenecks impede productivity in systematic parameter studies, motivating interest in automated workflows. This study presents CP-Agent, a harness-engineered LLM-based agent that autonomously executes complete CP modeling workflows from natural-language tasks. Operating under the ReAct paradigm, the agent reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness comprises a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic. CP-Agent is demonstrated on four case studies: calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress-strain and texture evolution; recovering the initial crystallographic texture of copper, where the agent correctly identifies a diffuse initial texture; and reproducing the multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, where the agent chains five deformation passes and recovers the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, robustly across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results. This work establishes harness engineering as a systematic approach to automating CP modeling workflows while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

infographic.key_insight: CP-Agent automates end-to-end crystal plasticity workflow execution from natural-language instructions by combining LLM reasoning with typed tools and external optimizers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It reduces manual effort in parameter calibration, multi-step simulation orchestration, and workflow reproducibility for polycrystalline metal modeling.
method: ReAct-based LLM agent with tool selection and sequencing.
Harness engineering with typed tool schemas, dispatcher, and safety-bounded iteration loop.
Delegates numerical search/calibration to established optimizers while keeping reasoning traces visible.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports four case studies—316L calibration, copper benchmark validation, initial texture recovery, and Mg-Zn-Ca rolling texture reproduction—with correct execution sequences and physically interpretable outputs across repeated runs.
infographic.watch_item: Performance still depends on tool quality, prompt/task specification, and bounded iteration settings, so robustness and failure modes should be checked in new workflows.
infographic.paper_title: CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows

title: A unified structure-preserving framework for geometric flows with coupled orientation and curvature dependence
authors: Yulin Zhang
abstract: We develop a structure-preserving parametric finite element framework for geometric flows whose energy density couples the unit normal and the curvature. This class includes bending energies with orientation-dependent rigidity or spontaneous curvature. A common fully discrete formulation treats closed curves in two dimensions and closed surfaces in three dimensions, and accommodates the $L^2$ flow, curve or surface diffusion, and the area- or volume-constrained $L^2$ flow. The formulation couples the geometric and curvature updates so that their contributions satisfy a discrete energy inequality. It uses continuous piecewise linear elements, a surface energy matrix, and a mass-lumped projection of the curvature derivative of the density. For positive densities satisfying a directional condition and convexity in curvature, we prove energy dissipation without a time-step restriction. The diffusion and constrained flows also preserve the enclosed area or volume exactly. The analysis allows non-even anisotropies and nonseparable dependence on orientation and curvature. Numerical experiments exhibit approximately second-order convergence in the manifold distance and confirm the discrete structural properties. Shape relaxation under an anisotropic Helfrich-type energy illustrates the use of the framework for coupled directional and bending effects.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a unified finite element framework that preserves geometric structure and energy dissipation for curve and surface flows with curvature-dependent and orientation-dependent bending energies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a reliable simulation tool for evolving interfaces in mechanics and materials where anisotropy, bending, and conservation of area or volume must be captured accurately.
method: Fully discrete parametric FEM for closed curves in 2D and closed surfaces in 3D
Couples geometric and curvature updates with a discrete energy inequality
Uses continuous piecewise linear elements, a surface energy matrix, and mass-lumped projection of curvature derivatives
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report approximately second-order convergence in manifold distance and verify the expected discrete energy dissipation and area/volume conservation properties.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on positive densities and a directional convexity condition in curvature, so highly nonconvex or poorly resolved anisotropic energies may require careful implementation.
infographic.paper_title: A unified structure-preserving framework for geometric flows with coupled orientation and curvature dependence

title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture
authors: D. M. LI, Meng-Cheng HE
abstract: Quasi-brittle fracture is prevalent in concrete, rock, ceramics, composites, and masonry, and its simulation faces a trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and simplicity. The classical Lattice Spring Model (LSM) captures cracking via bond breakage without remeshing, but its elements are empirical and limited to a few tessellable shapes with fixed Poisson's ratios. We propose a tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model (IELSM) that discretizes continua into polygonal elements with axial springs and a volumetric constraint, achieving isotropic elasticity on arbitrary polygonal tessellations. Macroscopic isotropy reduces to governing equations whose solvability gives a theoretical criterion for element admissibility, proving conventional tessellable elements and extending to arbitrary regular N-gons and concave elements. Exploiting boundary interpolation compatibility with finite elements, IELSM is assembled by direct node sharing, without interface elements or kinematic constraints. Coupled with an isotropic damage model, a pure bending test and four fracture benchmarks show that the coupling preserves displacement accuracy, yields crack paths and load-displacement curves agreeing with experiments and outperforming standard FEM, and is insensitive to mesh refinement. IELSM can also be restricted to damage-prone regions, with the remainder modeled by finite elements via node sharing. For the benchmarks, this reduces nodes by 41.2-80.9% and CPU time by 34.2-85.2% versus full-domain IELSM. The framework advances IELSM element construction from empirical trial and error to theoretical determination and simplifies coupling to node sharing, offering a balanced route for complex quasi-brittle fracture analysis.

infographic.key_insight: IELSM replaces trial-and-error lattice elements with a theoretically admissible, polygon-tessellated spring model that achieves isotropic elasticity and fracture simulation through simple node sharing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical way to model quasi-brittle cracking in concrete-like materials with better balance of accuracy, efficiency, and mesh compatibility than standard lattice models or full FEM.
method: Discretize the continuum into arbitrary polygonal tessellations with axial springs plus a volumetric constraint to enforce isotropic elasticity.
Derive admissible element shapes from governing equations, enabling regular N-gons and even concave elements.
Couple IELSM with FEM directly by shared nodes, and activate damage only in fracture-prone regions to reduce cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports pure bending and four fracture benchmarks where IELSM matches experiments and improves crack-path and load–displacement predictions, while hybridizing with FEM cuts nodes by 41.2–80.9% and CPU time by 34.2–85.2%.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on a theoretically admissible tessellation and an isotropic damage law, so element selection and parameter calibration may limit robustness for highly heterogeneous or strongly anisotropic materials.
infographic.paper_title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture

title: Concealing LLM-Based Multi-Agent Topology via Phantom Structure Injection
authors: Longzhu He, Zelang Wen, Xinfeng Li, Sen Su, XiaoFeng Wang
abstract: Driven by the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for collaborative reasoning over complex tasks. A key design element of MAS is the communication topology, which governs information flow among agents and often encodes proprietary knowledge about the system architecture. However, recent work has shown that such topologies can be inferred even in black-box settings by exploiting semantic dependencies in observable reasoning traces, posing significant risks of intellectual property leakage and exposure of system vulnerabilities. To address this threat, we propose MIRAGE, a topology-concealment framework that preserves the genuine communication topology for task execution while shaping adversary-facing semantic evidence toward a carefully constructed phantom topology. Specifically, MIRAGE operates in three stages: (1) phantom topology synthesis, (2) semantic edge realization, and (3) protected MAS execution. It constructs a phantom topology structurally distinct from the genuine one, materializes phantom edges as plausible semantic dependencies, and suppresses source-specific cues that could reveal genuine edges absent from the phantom topology. Extensive experiments across three topology optimization frameworks and four benchmark datasets demonstrate that MIRAGE substantially reduces the effectiveness of topology inference attacks while largely preserving the task utility of the protected MAS.

infographic.key_insight: MIRAGE hides an LLM multi-agent system’s true communication topology by making observed reasoning traces look like they come from a different, phantom topology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps protect proprietary MAS architectures and reduce vulnerability exposure when deploying collaborative LLM agents in security-sensitive engineering workflows.
method: Synthesize a phantom topology structurally different from the real one
Realize phantom edges through plausible semantic dependencies in agent traces
Suppress source-specific cues while preserving task execution on the genuine topology
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments across three topology-optimization frameworks and four benchmark datasets, showing strong reduction in topology-inference attack success with largely preserved task utility.
infographic.watch_item: The approach may add coordination complexity and could depend on careful tuning so that concealment does not degrade reasoning quality or introduce detectable artifacts.
infographic.paper_title: Concealing LLM-Based Multi-Agent Topology via Phantom Structure Injection

title: Hard-Trace First-Order Residual Learning for Coupled Stokes-Brinkman-Darcy Flow
authors: Zefeng Liu, Hongxing Rui
abstract: Stokes-Brinkman-Darcy (SBD) models connect free flow and porous flow through a Brinkman layer of finite thickness. The proposed method for solving these coupled equations consists of a mixed first-order formulation, shared interface traces and hard traction constraints, and a pressure correction based on boundary mass balance. Independent stresses, Darcy flux and pressure-gradient auxiliaries avoid second derivatives of network outputs. Boundary liftings and shared traces impose exterior and interface kinematic conditions exactly, while a stress map enforces native Brinkman-Darcy force balance. An integral momentum relation determines the pressure correction after training, without reference-pressure labels. Across two manufactured solutions and three permeabilities, mean corrected upper-pressure relative $L^2$ errors range from 0.87% to 2.58%; correction reduces both upper-pressure $L^2$ errors and the full Brinkman-pressure $H^1$ error in every run. Paired controls assess the contributions of interface sharing and traction enforcement. A non-manufactured filtration problem tests mixed-boundary adaptation against an independently refined finite-element reference, with all four runs satisfying the prescribed field and physical-consistency criteria.

infographic.key_insight: A hard-trace first-order neural formulation can solve coupled Stokes-Brinkman-Darcy flow by enforcing interface and boundary physics exactly while avoiding second derivatives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a physics-consistent surrogate for free-flow/porous-flow coupling with better pressure accuracy and a path to more reliable multiphysics simulations in filtration and porous media design.
method: Mixed first-order variables: stress, Darcy flux, and pressure-gradient auxiliaries remove second derivatives from the network.
Hard constraints: shared interface traces, boundary liftings, and traction maps enforce kinematic and force-balance conditions exactly.
Pressure correction: an integral momentum relation recovers pressure after training without reference-pressure labels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two manufactured tests and three permeabilities, corrected upper-pressure relative L2 error was 0.87%–2.58%, and correction improved both upper-pressure L2 and Brinkman-pressure H1 errors in every run; a filtration case also matched a refined FEM reference.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on careful construction of hard constraints and post-training pressure correction, so implementation complexity and sensitivity to interface/boundary specification may be a practical concern.
infographic.paper_title: Hard-Trace First-Order Residual Learning for Coupled Stokes-Brinkman-Darcy Flow

title: Automated Screw Planning for Reduced Pelvic Fractures Based on Statistical Shape Models and Deep Learning
authors: Yang Gao, Sutuke Yibulayimu, Yanzhen Liu, Zian Zhao, Yudi Sang
abstract: Percutaneous iliosacral screw fixation is an important minimally invasive treatment for unstable pelvic fractures. Because the sacroiliac region has complex anatomy and narrow screw corridors, the accuracy and safety of screw placement directly affect surgical outcomes. Accurate and reliable preoperative screw planning is therefore essential to improve surgical success and reduce intraoperative risks. Conventional preoperative planning typically requires surgeons to determine screw trajectories through manual measurements, a labor-intensive process that depends on subjective clinical experience. To address these challenges, we propose a fully automated pipeline for preoperative iliosacral screw planning in patients with pelvic fractures. Using patient-specific three-dimensional anatomy, the pipeline automatically identifies safe screw corridors and generates individualized insertion trajectories to support clinical preoperative planning. We evaluated the proposed pipeline on 200 clinical cases of pelvic fractures. Compared with conventional manual measurements, the safety margin of the safe insertion corridors increased by 2% across the four screw types, the mean planning time decreased by more than 90%, and the clinical acceptance rate reached 95%.

infographic.key_insight: A fully automated pipeline can plan patient-specific iliosacral screw trajectories for reduced pelvic fractures by identifying safe corridors from 3D anatomy, reducing manual planning burden while improving safety.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work supports faster and more reliable preoperative planning for minimally invasive pelvic fixation, where precise screw placement is critical to avoid neurovascular injury and failed fixation.
method: Uses patient-specific 3D anatomy from pelvic fracture cases
Combines statistical shape models with deep learning to detect safe screw corridors
Automatically generates individualized insertion trajectories for preoperative planning
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 200 clinical pelvic fracture cases, the method increased safe corridor margin by 2% across four screw types, cut planning time by over 90%, and achieved a 95% clinical acceptance rate.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on image quality and anatomical variability, so robust validation across diverse fracture patterns and imaging protocols is important before broad clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Screw Planning for Reduced Pelvic Fractures Based on Statistical Shape Models and Deep Learning

title: An augmented mixed finite element method for the Biot problem with nonlinear permeability
authors: Felipe Lepe, Gonzalo Rivera, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier, Segundo Villa-Fuentes
abstract: In two and three dimensions, we analyze a mixed formulation of the nonlinear Biot equations in terms of the poroelastic stress tensor, the displacement, the pressure, and the rotation tensor. To establish the well-posedness of the problem, we introduce suitable stabilization terms, leading to an augmented mixed formulation in which the associated parameters are chosen appropriately. Owing to the nonlinearity of the problem, we employ a fixed-point strategy to prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions. We propose a finite element scheme for which we establish existence and uniqueness of a discrete solution, together with a priori error estimates. Additionally, we design and analyze an a posteriori error estimator of the residual type which results to be reliable and efficient. Finally, we present a series of numerical experiments in two and three dimensions in order to assess the performance of the proposed method.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a stabilized augmented mixed finite element formulation for the nonlinear Biot poroelasticity problem, coupling stress, displacement, pressure, and rotation with a fixed-point treatment of nonlinear permeability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a mathematically well-posed and error-controlled framework for simulating coupled flow-deformation processes in porous media, which is important for geomechanics, subsurface engineering, and poromechanical design.
method: Augment the mixed Biot equations with suitable stabilization terms to ensure well-posedness.
Use a fixed-point strategy to handle the nonlinear permeability and prove existence/uniqueness.
Develop a finite element discretization with discrete solvability, a priori error estimates, and residual-based a posteriori estimators.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis plus two- and three-dimensional numerical experiments to assess performance, including reliability and efficiency of the residual estimator.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on carefully chosen stabilization parameters and fixed-point convergence, so practical implementation may be sensitive to parameter selection and nonlinear solve robustness.
infographic.paper_title: An augmented mixed finite element method for the Biot problem with nonlinear permeability

title: Growth-Inspired Graph Generation and Inverse Design of Mechanical Lattices via Dot Matrices Database Augmentation and GCNN
authors: Weiyun Xu, Jiamu Liu
abstract: Natural load-bearing and transport networks are not assembled in a single step; they emerge through a temporally ordered process of growth, branching, reinforcement, and loop formation. Inspired by this developmental logic, this work introduces a morphogenetic graph-generation framework for mechanical lattices in which a discrete dot matrix provides potential nodes and the final architecture is created by sequential cross-layer and intra-layer growth. The same rule is visualized in two dimensions as a leaf-vein-like developmental sequence and implemented in three dimensions on a 3x3x3 nodal matrix containing 27 candidate nodes. A dataset of distinct three-dimensional lattices was evaluated by beam-based finite element analysis and represented directly as graphs. A graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) with three graph-convolution layers and dual global pooling learns the topology-property mapping and predicts effective compressive stiffness. Coupling the GCNN surrogate with rapid structural sampling enables inverse design: for a target stiffness of 1000 MPa, the selected design was predicted at 1042.43 MPa and validated by finite element analysis at 1027.49 MPa. Beyond straight members, the framework has also been extended to parameterized horseshoe-shaped curved beams made of nonlinear materials, enabling topology-geometry design toward prescribed deformation shapes. Our work provides a paradigm for augmenting the database of mechanical metamaterials, and the resulting perspective links biological morphogenesis, graph learning, and nonlinear shape programming in a unified generative design framework for architected materials.

infographic.key_insight: A growth-inspired graph-generation strategy can synthesize mechanical lattices and pair them with a GCNN surrogate for fast inverse design of target stiffness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables rapid topology optimization of architected materials by reducing reliance on repeated finite element searches while still achieving close agreement with simulation.
method: Use a discrete dot-matrix node set and sequential cross-layer/intra-layer growth rules to generate lattice graphs.
Represent each lattice as a graph and train a 3-layer GCNN with dual global pooling to predict compressive stiffness.
Couple the surrogate with structural sampling for inverse design and extend the idea to curved, nonlinear beam geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports finite element evaluation of a 3x3x3 nodal matrix dataset and an inverse-design case where 1000 MPa target stiffness was predicted at 1042.43 MPa and validated at 1027.49 MPa.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the diversity and coverage of the generated lattice database, so generalization outside the sampled topology space should be checked carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Growth-Inspired Graph Generation and Inverse Design of Mechanical Lattices via Dot Matrices Database Augmentation and GCNN

title: Formation of shear bands through discrete localized plastic increments
authors: Heiner Olbermann, Hidde Schönberger
abstract: We study rate-independent systems in which the evolution is obtained by incremental minimization of elastic energy and one-homogeneous dissipation under constraints on the admissible inelastic increments. Such constraints arise naturally in several models of inelastic materials, including shear-transformation-zone models, intermittent plasticity, and quantized plasticity, where evolution proceeds through prescribed elementary activation events rather than arbitrary plastic increments. We establish the existence of a continuous-time limit for the corresponding constrained incremental scheme under suitable assumptions. As an application, we formulate a simplified shear-transformation-zone model consisting of localized activation events on a lattice embedded in a two-dimensional elastic medium. We prove that this model generates shear-band formation through the successive activation of neighboring transformation zones. More precisely, we show that every admissible evolution remains localized on a growing line segment in the infinite-domain setting and that the same mechanism persists on sufficiently large bounded domains. These results provide a rigorous mathematical framework for constrained activation models and show that restrictions on admissible elementary events alone constitute a mechanism for localization in rate-independent systems.

infographic.key_insight: Constrained, discrete plastic activation events in a rate-independent system can by themselves drive localized deformation and produce shear bands.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a rigorous basis for modeling localized plasticity and shear-band initiation in materials where inelastic evolution occurs through intermittent, quantized events rather than smooth flow.
method: Formulate rate-independent evolution as incremental minimization of elastic energy plus one-homogeneous dissipation.
Impose admissible increment constraints to represent localized activation events in shear-transformation zones.
Analyze a lattice-based 2D shear-transformation-zone model and prove localization along a growing line segment in the continuum limit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a mathematical existence result for the continuous-time limit and a proof that the model localizes into shear bands in both infinite-domain and sufficiently large bounded-domain settings.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is proven for a simplified constrained model, so transferring it to more detailed constitutive laws or finite meshes may require careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Formation of shear bands through discrete localized plastic increments
